transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thanks, doc. I appreciate it. I'll just get right to it, because, well, it's getting to be a real problem and I just don't know what's going on with me lately. What brings me in is I just keep forgetting things. And I don't mean normal things, like, you know, where I set my coffee mug down or where my keys are—I mean things I really, absolutely shouldn’t be forgetting. Important things. 

Like my heart follow-up appointments, for example. The cardiologist makes a big deal about it, says I need to come in to check on things, and I just completely miss it. Or the clinic will leave a message, and I think to myself, 'Okay, I need to call the clinic back right after lunch,' and then... nothing. It just completely vanishes from my mind until someone yells at me about it weeks later. 

And it's not just the medical stuff either, which is bad enough, believe me, but it's my everyday stuff too. Since I stopped working, I try to keep busy, do some repair jobs around the house or help out the neighbors, but I'll show up to fix something and realize I didn't bring the right tools. I'll get all the way under a sink or walk over to a buddy's garage, and I've got the completely wrong wrench, or I left the whole toolbox sitting on my kitchen table. It's just so frustrating, you know? You get all geared up to do a simple job, you know exactly what needs to be done, and your brain just skips a track and you're standing there empty-handed. I just can't keep dropping the ball on these things, so I figured I had to come talk to somebody.
About how long have you been experiencing these problems with your memory?

Well, let me think on that. I’d say it’s been causing real, actual trouble for about a year and two months now. Give or take a couple of weeks, but right around fourteen months. Because, see, that’s exactly when I had my cardiac scare. Oh boy, that was a whole ordeal. You think you’re perfectly fine, just going about your day, and suddenly the doctors are all hovering over you telling you that you need to take it easy. And I mean, I get it, they’re just doing their jobs, but taking it easy? That is just not how I’m wired. 

Before the heart thing, I was always, always on the move. I’d be out walking for miles every single morning, rain or shine, just wearing out the soles of my boots, or I’d be elbow-deep in these big projects. I’d be fixing up old engines, building shelves, helping the guys down the street with whatever they needed. And doing all that... it used to keep me settled, you know? Like, as long as my hands and my feet were busy, my brain worked just fine. It kept me grounded. 

But then this heart scare happens, and they forced me to cut way, way back on the walking and the projects. 'Sit in your recliner,' they said. 'Rest.' And I swear to you, doc, the minute I had to stop moving so much, it was like a switch flipped. Without all that activity to burn off whatever it is inside me, my brain just started spinning out of control and I started forgetting every little thing. So yeah, about a year and two months of this nonsense, all because I can't just get up and go like I used to.
Thinking back to when you were a kid or in school, did you ever have trouble with paying attention, being restless, or staying organized?

Well, now that you mention it... yeah. Yeah, I suppose I did. I mean, it’s funny you bring that up because I haven't thought about grade school in, well, decades. But, oh boy, my poor mother. She used to get so frustrated with me. I was that kid, you know? The one the teachers were always keeping an eye on. I just... I could not for the life of me stay in my seat. They’d tell us to sit and read, or practice our penmanship, and I’d be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or looking out the window, or walking over to see what Billy was doing two desks down. It was like the chair was made of hot coals. 

And the talking! I was always, always getting notes sent home pinned to my shirt because I was talking too much. 'He disrupts the class,' they’d write. Or 'He lacks self-control.' The teacher would ask a question to the whole room, and before she even finished the sentence, I’d just blurt out the answer. I didn't mean to be a nuisance, I really didn't, but my brain would just jump to the answer and my mouth would say it before I even remembered I was supposed to raise my hand. It was just... it was like I had a motor inside me that was always running a little too fast, even way back then. But, you know, back then they didn't really do anything about it, they just told you to straighten up or gave you a swat, and eventually, I just figured out how to keep myself busy with work and sports so I wouldn't get in trouble. But yeah, to answer your question, it was definitely an issue when I was a boy.
